jurisdictionNote: United States law only. Federal statutes are quoted from the Office of the Law Revision Counsel's U.S. Code; state examples come from the official code of the state named. State law varies, and nothing here is legal advice.

core: The felony/misdemeanor line is drawn by the term of imprisonment a legislature authorized, not by how serious the conduct feels
Federal classification under 18 U.S.C. 3559: Class A-E felonies, Class A-C misdemeanors, infractions
Sub-misdemeanor tiers that carry little or no jail exposure: infractions, violations, civil offenses, petty offenses
Grading and degrees within an offense, and what drives the grade (harm, mental state, victim characteristics, prior record, statutory aggravators)
Wobblers (alternative felony-misdemeanor offenses) and prosecutorial charging discretion as the practical determinant
The same conduct can be a felony in one state and a misdemeanor in another
Collateral consequences of a felony conviction: voting, firearms, occupational licensing, immigration, housing, benefits, employment screening
Case volume: misdemeanors and sub-misdemeanor offenses vastly outnumber felonies
supporting: Classification drives procedure, including the Sixth Amendment jury-trial line at six months (Lewis v. United States)
Federal fine tiers keyed to offense class (18 U.S.C. 3571)
Federal law sometimes keys consequences to a state's own label (21 U.S.C. 862a) and sometimes overrides it (18 U.S.C. 921(a)(20)(B), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(43))
outOfScope: The criminal/civil distinction, burdens of proof, and parallel civil liability (owned by criminal-law-versus-civil-law)
Actus reus, mens rea, causation, and concurrence as elements (owned by elements-of-a-crime)
Sentencing structure, guidelines, mandatory minimums, and sentencing hearings (owned by trial-and-sentencing)
Juvenile adjudication categories, expungement and record-sealing procedure, and any individualized advice about a person's record or rights

claims.claim: Federal law classifies an offense not specifically graded in the statute defining it by the maximum term of imprisonment authorized: life or death is a Class A felony, twenty-five years or more a Class B felony, ten to under twenty-five a Class C felony, five to under ten a Class D felony, more than one year to under five a Class E felony; one year or less but more than six months is a Class A misdemeanor, six months or less but more than thirty days a Class B misdemeanor, thirty days or less but more than five days a Class C misdemeanor, and five days or less (or no authorized imprisonment) an infraction.

The classifying fact is the punishment authorized by statute, not the sentence a particular defendant receives; New York draws the same one-year line, defining a felony as an offense for which a sentence to a term of imprisonment in excess of one year may be imposed and a misdemeanor as one permitting more than fifteen days but not more than one year.

Below the misdemeanor tier sit offenses with little or no jail exposure: a federal infraction authorizes five days or less or no imprisonment at all; New York's 'violation' is an offense for which a sentence in excess of fifteen days cannot be imposed and is not a crime, since New York defines 'crime' as a misdemeanor or a felony; California classifies some offenses as infractions rather than misdemeanors.

Federal law defines a 'petty offense' as a Class B misdemeanor, a Class C misdemeanor, or an infraction whose maximum fine does not exceed the amounts in 18 U.S.C. 3571(b)(6)-(7) for individuals or 3571(c)(6)-(7) for organizations; those paragraphs cap the fine at $5,000 for an individual convicted of a Class B or C misdemeanor not resulting in death, and $5,000 for an infraction.

Classification drives procedure as well as punishment: the Supreme Court held in Lewis v. United States, 518 U.S. 322 (1996), that an offense carrying a maximum prison term of six months or less is presumed petty and carries no Sixth Amendment jury-trial right, and that the right does not attach merely because charges aggregated in one proceeding could exceed six months.

Legislatures grade within an offense as well as across offenses. Federal murder is divided by mental state and circumstance rather than by outcome: killing by poison, lying in wait, or other willful, deliberate, malicious and premeditated killing, or killing during an enumerated felony such as arson, kidnapping, burglary or robbery, is first-degree murder, and any other murder is second-degree murder.

New York classifies felonies for sentencing purposes into five categories (Class A, subdivided into A-I and A-II, plus Classes B, C, D and E) and misdemeanors into three (Class A, Class B, and unclassified), showing that letter grading is a state as well as a federal drafting technique.

California recognizes 'wobblers': when a crime is punishable in the court's discretion either by state prison or county jail under Penal Code section 1170(h) or by fine or county jail, it is a misdemeanor for all purposes if, among other routes, the prosecutor files a misdemeanor complaint or the court declares the offense a misdemeanor at probation or before trial. General grand theft is such an offense, punishable by county jail not exceeding one year or pursuant to section 1170(h).

Charging discretion is the practical determinant of the grade in wobbler cases. Federal charging policy instructs prosecutors to select the most appropriate charges, ordinarily including the most serious offense encompassed by the conduct that is likely to result in a sustainable conviction, while weighing proportionality through an individualized assessment.

The same conduct can carry different labels in different states. Theft of goods worth $980 exceeds California's $950 petty-theft ceiling and so may be charged as grand theft, an offense punishable as a felony or a misdemeanor; the same theft in Virginia falls below the $1,000 grand-larceny threshold and is petit larceny, a Class 1 misdemeanor.

Federal firearm law keys its prohibition to authorized punishment rather than to a state's label: 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(1) makes it unlawful for a person convicted of a crime punishable by imprisonment for a term exceeding one year to possess a firearm, and 18 U.S.C. 921(a)(20)(B) excludes from that phrase any state offense classified by the state as a misdemeanor and punishable by two years or less.

Immigration consequences can turn on the sentence rather than the state label: the 'aggravated felony' definition applies to listed offenses whether in violation of federal or state law, and several entries (a crime of violence, a theft or burglary offense) turn on a term of imprisonment of at least one year; separately, a noncitizen is deportable for a crime involving moral turpitude committed within five years of admission for which a sentence of one year or longer may be imposed, or for an aggravated felony at any time after admission.

Some federal benefit bars key expressly to the state's own classification: 21 U.S.C. 862a denies TANF assistance and SNAP benefits to a person convicted of an offense 'classified as a felony by the law of the jurisdiction involved' that has as an element the possession, use, or distribution of a controlled substance, subject to state opt-out or limitation by a law enacted after August 22, 1996.

Federal housing regulations require public housing agencies in the Housing Choice Voucher program to bar admission of any household containing a member subject to a lifetime state sex-offender registration requirement, and to bar admission where a household member has ever been convicted of manufacturing methamphetamine on federally assisted premises; other criminal activity supports permissive denial.

State approaches to felony disenfranchisement vary sharply. As summarized by NCSL on May 20, 2026: in the District of Columbia, Maine and Vermont people convicted of felonies never lose the vote; in 23 states rights are lost only during incarceration and restored automatically on release; in 15 states they are also lost during parole and/or probation; and in 10 states rights are lost indefinitely for some crimes or require a pardon, a waiting period, or additional action.

Collateral consequences are numerous and are catalogued jurisdiction by jurisdiction. Compiling the National Inventory of Collateral Consequences of Conviction as of February 2019, the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights counted approximately 44,631 collateral consequences, of which nearly 40 percent (17,436) are triggered by any felony conviction and about 19 percent (8,294) by any misdemeanor, and reported that roughly 70 percent of the more than 44,000 state and federal consequences relate to employment.

A criminal record is not itself a protected characteristic, but federal enforcement guidance treats criminal-record screens as subject to Title VII disparate-impact analysis: an exclusion based on an arrest alone is not job related and consistent with business necessity, while conviction records must be assessed against the nature and gravity of the offense, the time elapsed, and the nature of the job.

The lower tiers carry the caseload. In California superior courts in fiscal year 2022-23 there were 3,243,657 criminal filings: 183,151 felonies (5.6 percent), 338,714 misdemeanors (262,034 nontraffic plus 76,680 traffic; 10.4 percent), and 2,721,792 infractions (177,007 nontraffic plus 2,544,785 traffic; 83.9 percent). Misdemeanors were about 65 percent of felony-plus-misdemeanor filings, roughly 1.85 misdemeanors for every felony.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a single national count of misdemeanor cases can be stated
positions: Commonly cited national estimates of roughly 13 million annual misdemeanor filings come from scholarly reconstructions of incomplete state-court data.
The National Center for State Courts' Court Statistics Project reports state-court caseloads, but its felony/misdemeanor breakdown was not retrievable from the live site during this research session.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not assert a national misdemeanor count. It uses one complete, dated, official state series (California superior courts, FY2022-23) to show the shape of the caseload and says plainly that this is one state's data and that other states count differently.

positions: The NICCC site itself publishes no running total on its public pages.
The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, compiling NICCC data as of February 2019, reported approximately 44,631.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the 44,631 figure with its February 2019 date and its source, and frames it as a snapshot of a database that changes with legislation rather than a fixed count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the felony/misdemeanor label is decisive for consequences
positions: Some federal consequences key expressly to the state's own label (21 U.S.C. 862a).
Others override the label and key to authorized punishment or to the sentence imposed (18 U.S.C. 921(a)(20)(B); 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(43)).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both patterns explicitly rather than presenting the label as uniformly controlling.
